34: ## 2. OVERVIEW
35: 
36: ### Why This Skill Exists
37: 
38: Some failures repeat. Someone edits a file they never opened. Someone reports a green test run nobody watched finish. Someone deletes a migration with no way back. Catching those in review costs the same amount every time, so writing the constraint down where it loads at the moment of the action is cheaper.
39: 
40: The trouble is that rule sets rot in a specific way. They only ever grow. Every plausible suggestion becomes a file, the set reaches forty entries and nobody reads any of them. A set that grows because more rules feel thorough has already failed. This skill exists to hold that line, which is why it refuses most of what it is asked for.
41: 
42: ### What A Repo Rule Is
43: 
44: A rule constrains how you do something. It loads when you are about to take a particular action and tells you what you may not do while taking it.
45: 
46: That makes it different from a skill. A skill loads when you need a capability and teaches you how. A rule loads when you are already working and narrows your options.
47: 
48: One question settles most cases. **If it tells you how to accomplish something it is a skill. If it tells you what you may not do while accomplishing it, it is a rule.**
49: 
50: ### How A Rule Reaches You
51: 
52: Rules do not all load at once. The repository root holds `REPO RULES.md`, a router with a trigger table. Each row lists actions on the left and one rule file on the right.
53: 
54: 1. You are about to take an action, say deleting a file or reporting a result.
55: 2. You match that action against the trigger table. The action, never the topic of the request.
56: 3. You open every rule file that row names and follow it.
57: 4. Two rows match, so you load both. No row matches, so nothing loads and you do not go looking for a rule to apply.
58: 
59: The load is mandatory. What you load is not the top of the ladder. A rule sits below `AGENTS.md` and below a live instruction from you. Where a rule and `AGENTS.md` appear to disagree, `AGENTS.md` wins, the rule is wrong and the right response is to say so rather than follow it.
60: 
61: That ordering earns its keep. A rule set that could override the harness would need a review process before anyone touched it. One that cannot be overridden can be edited freely, which is what makes the next part workable.
62: 
63: ### Rules Are Meant To Change
64: 
65: A rule supplements the harness. It carries a `version` because it will change. It should be removed once nothing it prevents still happens.
66: 
67: This skill owns all three moves. A create mode that cannot delete produces a set nobody prunes, and an unpruned set is one nobody reads.
68:

77: ```bash

79: ```

87: ```

93: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
94: 
95: The four decision tests load on every path, including retirement, because "should this exist" and "should this still exist" are the same four questions.
96: 
97: - **Test 1** asks what must bind on a turn where no trigger fires. Content that holds unconditionally cannot live behind a trigger, so it belongs in `AGENTS.md` instead.
98: - **Test 2** checks the router's scope statement, which puts routing out of bounds: which skill, which command, which model, which flags.
99: - **Test 3** runs four conditions covering single rows, content another rule already carries and proposals with nothing to load them.
100: - **Test 4** asks what fails today without the rule.
101: 
102: Survive all four and the anatomy reference and template load. You fill ten fixed elements:
103: 
104: - six-key frontmatter in one order
105: - a title line
106: - a routed-from line
107: - a line stating the rule expands `AGENTS.md` and never overrides it
108: - the actions that fire it
109: - one bold sentence carrying the obligation
110: - a numbered body in capitals
111: - one divider per numbered section
112: - a closing self-check
113: - a link back to the router
114: 
115: Then five reader tests decide whether the draft earns its load. Structure is checkable and it is not the bar. A rule can satisfy every assertion above and still say nothing you would change your behaviour over. None of those five can be automated, so a person has to read the draft and answer them.
116: 
117: Wiring comes last: a trigger row, an index row and a pointer from each `AGENTS.md` section the rule governs.
118: 
119: ### Key Concept: Order Protects The Half-Finished State
120: 
121: Create writes the file first, then the rows. Retire removes them in exactly the reverse order: pointer, index row, trigger row, then the file.
122: 
123: Both orderings answer the same question. What does an interrupted run leave behind? Write the file first and the worst case is a file nothing points at, which is inert and obvious. Add the row first and the worst case is a router row pointing at nothing, which reads as working coverage to anyone who looks. Always leave the safer wreck.

128: 
129: ### When To Use This Skill
130: 
131: Reach for create-repo-rule when someone describes a recurring failure and wants it stopped, when an existing rule no longer matches how the work is done, when a rule has stopped earning its load or when a repository needs a rule router because it has none.
132:

146: ## 6. TROUBLESHOOTING
147: 
148: | What you see | Why | Fix |
149: |---|---|---|
150: | Your request was refused and you disagree | Most requests are refused by design, usually on test 1 | Read which test refused it. The destination it names is generally a better home than a new file |
151: | A rule was written but never fires | It has a file and no trigger row, or the row describes a topic rather than an action | Check the router for a matching row, then check that the row lists actions you take |
152: | The router points at a file that does not exist | A retirement removed the file before the row | Remove the row too, then run the count check in section 8. Rows and files must match |
153: | A trigger phrase reaches the wrong rule | Two rules claim the same phrase | Sweep for duplicates. The set carries 161 phrases with zero collisions, so any duplicate is a defect |
154: | `validate_document.py --type reference` calls a rule invalid | A repo rule has no Overview section by design, and that type requires one | Use the structural check in section 8. All nine shipped rules fail that document type for this same reason |
155: | The draft passes every check and still reads as filler | Structure is checkable and it is not the bar | Run the five reader tests in `creation-standards.md`. They need a person, not a script |
156: 
157: ---
158: 
159: ## 7. FAQ
160: 
161: **Q: Why does it refuse so much?**
162: 
163: A: Because the alternative is a set nobody reads. Every rule you add raises the cost of loading the set and lowers the odds any single rule gets read. "Best practice" and "we might need it later" are the exact phrases that produce forty unread files.
164: 
165: **Q: My rule is correct. Why does test 1 still refuse it?**
166: 
167: A: Correctness is not what test 1 measures. It asks whether the content must bind when no trigger has fired. A rule that must always hold, filed behind a trigger, stops holding on every turn that trigger misses. It looks present in the repository and is absent in practice.
168: 
169: **Q: Can a rule override `AGENTS.md`?**
170: 
171: A: No, and the refusal is the useful part. Where they appear to disagree, the rule is wrong. Say so rather than following it.
172: 
173: **Q: What happens if the repository has no `REPO RULES.md`?**
174: 
175: A: The router gets emitted first, from a template. No router means no rule can load, whatever else is true. It is a prerequisite rather than the thing you asked for, and it gets reported that way.
176: 
177: **Q: How long should a rule be?**
178: 
179: A: At or under 160 lines is preferred and most subjects fit. 161 to 200 is fine without comment. 201 to 250 is allowed when the rule can say why it needs the room. Over 250 means splitting it or cutting it. Three of the nine shipped rules sit at the limit, and each absorbed content moved down from `AGENTS.md`, so their length is explained rather than accidental.
180: 
181: **Q: Is a refusal a dead end?**
182: 
183: A: No. Every refusal except the restraint one names a destination. The restraint refusal routes nowhere on purpose, and its recorded reason is the deliverable, so the same proposal does not arrive next quarter with nobody remembering why it was declined.

129: ### When To Use This Skill
130: 
131: Reach for create-repo-rule when someone describes a recurring failure and wants it stopped, when an existing rule no longer matches how the work is done, when a rule has stopped earning its load or when a repository needs a rule router because it has none.
132: 
133: Skip it when the request teaches a capability rather than constraining one, when the content must bind on every turn or when the request is about which skill or command to route to.
134: 
135: ### Related Skills
136: 
137: | Skill | Relationship |
138: |---|---|
139: | `sk-create-skill` | Owns capability authoring. A skill teaches how, a rule constrains what you may not do |
140: | `sk-create-command` | Owns the `/create:repo-rule` command surface that invokes this mode |
141: | `sk-create-manual-testing-playbook` | Owns the playbook contract this packet's `manual-testing-playbook/` follows |
142: | `system-spec-kit` | Owns spec-folder documentation, which sits outside the rule set entirely |
143:

145: 
146: ## 6. TROUBLESHOOTING
147: 
148: | What you see | Why | Fix |
149: |---|---|---|
150: | Your request was refused and you disagree | Most requests are refused by design, usually on test 1 | Read which test refused it. The destination it names is generally a better home than a new file |
151: | A rule was written but never fires | It has a file and no trigger row, or the row describes a topic rather than an action | Check the router for a matching row, then check that the row lists actions you take |
152: | The router points at a file that does not exist | A retirement removed the file before the row | Remove the row too, then run the count check in section 8. Rows and files must match |
153: | A trigger phrase reaches the wrong rule | Two rules claim the same phrase | Sweep for duplicates. The set carries 161 phrases with zero collisions, so any duplicate is a defect |
154: | `validate_document.py --type reference` calls a rule invalid | A repo rule has no Overview section by design, and that type requires one | Use the structural check in section 8. All nine shipped rules fail that document type for this same reason |
155: | The draft passes every check and still reads as filler | Structure is checkable and it is not the bar | Run the five reader tests in `creation-standards.md`. They need a person, not a script |
156: 
157: ---
158: 
159: ## 7. FAQ
160: 
161: **Q: Why does it refuse so much?**
162: 
163: A: Because the alternative is a set nobody reads. Every rule you add raises the cost of loading the set and lowers the odds any single rule gets read. "Best practice" and "we might need it later" are the exact phrases that produce forty unread files.
164: 
165: **Q: My rule is correct. Why does test 1 still refuse it?**
166: 
167: A: Correctness is not what test 1 measures. It asks whether the content must bind when no trigger has fired. A rule that must always hold, filed behind a trigger, stops holding on every turn that trigger misses. It looks present in the repository and is absent in practice.
168: 
169: **Q: Can a rule override `AGENTS.md`?**
170: 
171: A: No, and the refusal is the useful part. Where they appear to disagree, the rule is wrong. Say so rather than following it.
172: 
173: **Q: What happens if the repository has no `REPO RULES.md`?**
174: 
175: A: The router gets emitted first, from a template. No router means no rule can load, whatever else is true. It is a prerequisite rather than the thing you asked for, and it gets reported that way.
176: 
177: **Q: How long should a rule be?**
178: 
179: A: At or under 160 lines is preferred and most subjects fit. 161 to 200 is fine without comment. 201 to 250 is allowed when the rule can say why it needs the room. Over 250 means splitting it or cutting it. Three of the nine shipped rules sit at the limit, and each absorbed content moved down from `AGENTS.md`, so their length is explained rather than accidental.
180: 
181: **Q: Is a refusal a dead end?**
182: 
183: A: No. Every refusal except the restraint one names a destination. The restraint refusal routes nowhere on purpose, and its recorded reason is the deliverable, so the same proposal does not arrive next quarter with nobody remembering why it was declined.

94:     "REVISE": ["references/rule-anatomy.md", "references/agents-md-integration.md"],

112:     resolved = (SKILL_ROOT / relative_path).resolve()
113:     resolved.relative_to(SKILL_ROOT)

119:     guarded = _guard_in_skill(relative_path)

141:     scores = score_intents(request)

144:         return {

146:             "needs_disambiguation": True,
147:             "disambiguation_checklist": UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST,
148:             "resources": loaded,
149:         }
150: 
151:     intent = max(scores, key=scores.get)                      # Tier 2: happy path
152:     if target_repo_has_no_router():
153:         load_if_available("assets/repo-rules-router-template.md", inventory, loaded, seen)
154:     for resource in RESOURCE_MAP[intent]:

8: # create-repo-rule
9: 
10: `create-repo-rule` is the repo-rule authoring workflow packet of the `sk-doc` family. It
11: turns a user's request — a behaviour they want, or a failure they keep hitting — into a
12: file in the target repository's rules directory (`.skilled/repo-rules/` where a `.skilled`
13: source root exists, `repo-rules/` otherwise), wired into its `REPO RULES.md` router.
14: 
15: **Most requests should not become a rule.** The four decision tests in
16: `references/decision-tests.md` refuse more than they admit, and running them first is the
17: cheap order. Authoring a rule that then fails a test is the expensive one.
18: 
19: A repo rule **supplements the harness**. It sits below `AGENTS.md` and below a live
20: operator instruction, it can be changed when it stops matching the work, and it can be
21: removed when it stops earning its load. This mode owns all three.
22:

17: # Integration and Lifecycle: Wiring, Revising and Retiring a Rule
18: 
19: A rule file that nothing points at is inert.
20: 
21: ---
22: 
23: ## 1. OVERVIEW
24: 
25: The router's trigger table is the only thing that **loads** one; the pointer from the
26: governed `AGENTS.md` section is the only thing that makes it **findable at the moment
27: of need**.
28: 
29: **When to Use**:
30: 
31: - Wiring an accepted rule: the trigger row, the index row and the governed-section pointer.
32: - Revising a rule, especially when the firing condition changed.
33: - Retiring a rule, in the order that leaves nothing pointing at a deleted file.
34: 
35: ---
36: 
37: ## 2. THE THREE WIRING POINTS
38: 
39: | Point | Where | Lost without it |
40: |-------|-------|-----------------|
41: | **Trigger row** | `REPO RULES.md` §2 | The rule never loads. Nothing else in the system fires a rule file |
42: | **Index row** | `REPO RULES.md` §3 | The rule is unbrowsable — reachable only by already knowing its trigger |
43: | **Governed-section pointer** | The `AGENTS.md` section it expands | The rule is discoverable at session start and invisible at the moment of need. This is the one people skip |
44: 
45: **Required:** every shipped rule has its trigger row and its index row, and
46: `check-repo-rules.cjs` fails the corpus when either is missing.
47: 
48: - **A rule that expands an `AGENTS.md` section** gets a pointer there, and a rule
49:   governing two areas gets one in each. The governed-section pointer is the default, not
50:   a gate.
51: - **A rule whose subject no `AGENTS.md` section states** is reached through its trigger
52:   row alone.
53: 
54: Count the live pointers with `grep -c <rule-file> AGENTS.md` rather than trusting a number
55: written here.
56: 
57: ---
58: 
59: ## 3. THE SCOPE-STATEMENT CHECK — RUN IT FIRST
60: 
61: Before adding a trigger row, confirm `REPO RULES.md` §4 **In** admits the rule.
62: 
63: The shipped set hit this four times, and every time the row was written before
64: anyone looked:
65: 
66: - Adding the delegation rule under a scope statement that listed "agent dispatch" as
67:   **Out**. The router would have routed to a rule it declared out of bounds.
68: - Moving communication down while §4 said nothing about how a reply reads.
69: 
70: All four were caught and the boundary was widened deliberately each time, the third
71: being the narrow routing carve-out that admits verifying wiring you changed while still
72: refusing route selection.
73: 
74: **A fifth widening that admitted selection itself would dissolve the boundary the set
75: exists to hold:** if the scope statement excludes a proposal, that is a refusal, not a
76: paperwork problem. The mode does not widen §4 unilaterally; that is an operator decision,
77: and each of the four was one.
78: 
79: ---
80: 
81: ## 4. CREATE
82: 
83: Order matters, and it is chosen so an interruption is survivable. A repository with no
84: `REPO RULES.md` gets its router emitted first, from `assets/repo-rules-router-template.md`
85: (§8), because no router means no rule can load.
86: 
87: 1. **Scope check** (§3 above). Refuse here if it fails.
88: 2. **Write the rule file.** First, deliberately.
89: 3. **Add the trigger row.**
90: 4. **Add the index row.**
91: 5. **Add the pointer** to each `AGENTS.md` section the rule governs.
92: 6. **Verify**: every link resolves; trigger rows, index rows and rule files are all the
93:    same count.
94: 
95: **Why the file first.** Stop after step 2 and you have an unreferenced file — inert,
96: harmless, obvious. Stop after step 3 with no file and you have a router row pointing at
97: nothing, which **looks like coverage**. Always leave the safer wreck.
98: 
99: ---
100: 
101: ## 5. REVISE
102: 
103: 1. Run the decision tests again. A rule that no longer passes them should be **retired,
104:    not patched** — a rule kept alive by editing is how a set stops meaning anything.
105: 2. Edit the rule.
106: 3. **If the change alters when the rule fires, change the trigger row in the same edit.**
107:    Otherwise the router now lies about the rule, and it lies silently.
108: 4. Bump `version`.
109: 5. Re-verify links and counts.
110: 
111: **On `version`:** use the fourth segment for any content change and leave the first three
112: alone until something forces the question. **This is a choice, not a finding.**
113: 
114: ---
115: 
116: ## 6. RETIRE
117: 
118: **The rule set has never done this.** The path below is the create path inverted, and it
119: has been dry-run rather than performed.
120: 
121: 1. **Remove the pointer** from every governed `AGENTS.md` section.
122: 2. **Remove the index row.**
123: 3. **Remove the trigger row.** The rule can no longer load.
124: 4. **Delete the file.**
125: 5. **Record why**, so the same rule is not proposed again next quarter with nobody
126:    remembering it was refused.
127: 6. **Verify**: counts equal again, every remaining link resolves.

16: # Creation Standards: Is This Rule Worth Loading?
17: 
18: `rule-anatomy.md` decides whether a file is *shaped* like a rule. That is checkable and it
19: is not enough — a rule can satisfy every structural assertion and say nothing a reader
20: would change their behaviour over.
21: 
22: ---
23: 
24: ## 1. OVERVIEW
25: 
26: These five tests are read out of what the shipped corpus already does. Every one passes
27: across the corpus. Each is a question a reviewer answers by reading; none can be automated, and
28: that limit is the reason they live here rather than in the structural floor.
29: 
30: **When to Use**:
31: 
32: - Before finishing a draft rule, once it is shaped like a rule.
33: - Reviewing a rule that passes every structural check and still reads as filler.
34: - Deciding whether a section, a trigger phrase, a binding sentence, a self-check item or a misreading guard earns its place.
35: 
36: **Not a gate on whether the rule may exist**: that is `decision-tests.md`, and it runs
37: first. These standards assume the rule has already earned the right to be written.
38: 
39: ---
40: 
41: ## 2. THE SECTION TEST
42: 
43: **A numbered section earns its place by making clear what goes wrong without it.**
44: 
45: This is the test the corpus meets least obviously and most consistently. The corpus splits
46: between rules that state it outright with a `The failure this prevents:` line and rules that
47: carry it in the section's substance instead:
48: 
49: - `evidence-and-proof.md` §3 is titled **THE FOUR WAYS A GREEN RUN LIES** and then
50:   enumerates them. The section *is* the failure.
51: - `uncertainty-and-honesty.md` §3 says "agreeing for conversational flow is a failure
52:   mode, not politeness" and "praise that is not earned makes the earned kind worthless".
53: - `blast-radius.md` §2 prices every tier by **cost when wrong**.
54: 
55: **So the standard is the identifiability, not the sentence.** An explicit
56: `The failure this prevents:` line is a good habit and not a requirement; a section whose
57: substance is the failure has already met the test.
58: 
59: **The check:** read the section and say aloud what breaks without it. If you cannot,
60: the section is a topic rather than a rule, and it goes.
61: 
62: > A grep cannot run this test. An early attempt to measure it by pattern reported only the
63: > most recently written rules as compliant, because they happened to share a phrasing. The
64: > corpus was fine; the measurement was wrong.
65: 
66: ---
67: 
68: ## 3. THE TRIGGER-PHRASE TEST
69: 
70: **Phrases are what someone types when they have the problem, not what the section is called.**
71: 
72: Section titles are already greppable from the body. A phrase earns its place by catching a
73: reader who has the problem and does not know the rule exists.
74: 
75: | Good | Useless |
76: |------|---------|
77: | "it's a flake" | "root cause methodology" |
78: | "while I was in there" | "scope management" |
79: | "might need it later" | "the restraint ladder" |
80: 
81: **Two hard constraints:**
82: 
83: - **No phrase may appear in two rules.** The set carries 255 phrases across the 13 files
84:   in the rules directory (`.skilled/repo-rules/`) with zero collisions. A duplicate
85:   makes both rules unfindable by it.
86: - **One phrase per distinct symptom, with no count target.** The rules carry 16 to 29.
87:   Too few leaves a rule hard to reach. A long list usually means section titles crept
88:   back in, so check that each phrase is something a person types when they have the
89:   problem.
90: 
91: ---
92: 
93: ## 4. THE BINDING-SENTENCE TEST
94: 
95: **One sentence, one obligation.**
96: 
97: If the binding sentence needs a conjunction to hold two demands, it is either two rules or
98: one vaguer rule than you actually have. Check by removing everything after the "and" — if
99: what remains is still the rule, the second half belonged in a section.
100: 
101: A binding sentence that could be printed on its own and still direct behaviour has passed.
102: One that only makes sense after reading the body has not.
103: 
104: ---
105: 
106: ## 5. THE SELF-CHECK TEST
107: 
108: **One item per obligation the body creates — never one per section.**
109: 
110: A self-check that mirrors the section titles is a table of contents with checkboxes. It
111: tells a reader what the rule contains, which they can see, instead of what they must have
112: done, which is the point.
113: 
114: Observed range is 5-11 items, and it does not track section count: `prevent-overengineering.md`
115: has 6 sections and 5 items; `delegation-and-orchestration.md` has 9 sections and 11. The
116: number follows the obligations, not the structure.
117: 
118: **The check:** for each item, name the sentence in the body that created that obligation.
119: An item with no such sentence is decoration; a body obligation with no item is a gap.
120: 
121: ---
122: 
123: ## 6. THE MISREADING GUARD
124: 
125: **A rule that could be read as licence to do less needs a section saying it is not.**
126: 
127: Some rules in the corpus carry a `WHAT THIS RULE IS NOT` section, and the pattern is instructive —
128: the examples below are rules whose surface reading permits *less* work:
129: 
130: | Rule | The misreading it refuses |
131: |------|---------------------------|
132: | `prevent-overengineering.md` | "build less" becoming licence to under-deliver frozen scope |
133: | `delegation-and-orchestration.md` | "orchestrate it" becoming licence to delegate everything |
134: | `communication.md` | "match length to the question" becoming licence to omit what the reader needs |
135: | `communication-decisions.md` | "verdict first" becoming licence to reason less before writing |
136: | `communication-handoff.md` | "name what is left" becoming licence to ask more, or to hand back your own unfinished work |
137: 
138: Rules without one are rules that only ever demand *more* rigour — nobody misreads
139: "fix the producer, not the symptom" as permission to do less.
140: 
141: **The check:** could a tired reader use this rule as an excuse? If yes, refuse that reading
142: explicitly. If no, the section would be ceremony.
143: 
144: ---
145: 
146: ## 7. DON'TS
147: 
148: Each is an observed failure, not a preference.
149: 
150: - **Don't cite a best practice without naming what it prevents.** `AGENTS.md` forbids this
151:   everywhere else; a rule that does it is holding others to a bar it fails.
152: - **Don't restate another rule.** Link instead — and expect not to need to.
153: - **Don't write a rule that fires on a topic.** Triggers are actions you are about to take.
154:   A rule that fires on "thinking about testing" fires never.
155: - **Don't add a section because the rule looks short.** Length is not the target.
156: - **Don't write the self-check last and fastest.** It is the part a reader actually uses
157:   under time pressure, and it is where a rule most often stops being actionable.
158: 
159: ---
160: 
161: ## 8. WHAT THIS DOCUMENT IS NOT
162: 
163: - **Not a scoring rubric.** There is no number. Every test needs a reader, and a checkable
164:   proxy would measure the proxy.
165: - **Not licence to hold a draft to a bar the corpus does not meet.** Every test here passes
166:   on every shipped rule. A proposed sixth standard that they fail is a wrong standard.
167: 
168: ---
169: 
170: ## 9. SELF-CHECK
171: 
172: - [ ] For every section, I can say what breaks without it.
173: - [ ] No trigger phrase of mine appears in another rule.
174: - [ ] The binding sentence holds one obligation and stands alone.
175: - [ ] Every self-check item traces to a sentence in the body that created it.
176: - [ ] If the rule could be read as licence to do less, it says it is not.
177: - [ ] No best practice is cited without the failure it prevents.

73: reader who has the problem and does not know the rule exists.
74: 
75: | Good | Useless |
76: |------|---------|
77: | "it's a flake" | "root cause methodology" |
78: | "while I was in there" | "scope management" |
79: | "might need it later" | "the restraint ladder" |

81: **Two hard constraints:**
82: 
83: - **No phrase may appear in two rules.** The set carries 255 phrases across the 13 files
84:   in the rules directory (`.skilled/repo-rules/`) with zero collisions. A duplicate
85:   makes both rules unfindable by it.
86: - **One phrase per distinct symptom, with no count target.** The rules carry 16 to 29.
87:   Too few leaves a rule hard to reach. A long list usually means section titles crept
88:   back in, so check that each phrase is something a person types when they have the
89:   problem.
90: 
91: ---
92: 
93: ## 4. THE BINDING-SENTENCE TEST
94: 
95: **One sentence, one obligation.**
96: 
97: If the binding sentence needs a conjunction to hold two demands, it is either two rules or
98: one vaguer rule than you actually have. Check by removing everything after the "and" — if
99: what remains is still the rule, the second half belonged in a section.
100: 
101: A binding sentence that could be printed on its own and still direct behaviour has passed.
102: One that only makes sense after reading the body has not.
103: 
104: ---
105: 
106: ## 5. THE SELF-CHECK TEST
107: 
108: **One item per obligation the body creates — never one per section.**
109: 
110: A self-check that mirrors the section titles is a table of contents with checkboxes. It
111: tells a reader what the rule contains, which they can see, instead of what they must have
112: done, which is the point.
113: 
114: Observed range is 5-11 items, and it does not track section count: `prevent-overengineering.md`
115: has 6 sections and 5 items; `delegation-and-orchestration.md` has 9 sections and 11. The
116: number follows the obligations, not the structure.
117: 
118: **The check:** for each item, name the sentence in the body that created that obligation.
119: An item with no such sentence is decoration; a body obligation with no item is a gap.
120: 
121: ---
122: 
123: ## 6. THE MISREADING GUARD
124: 
125: **A rule that could be read as licence to do less needs a section saying it is not.**
126:

128: the examples below are rules whose surface reading permits *less* work:
129: 
130: | Rule | The misreading it refuses |
131: |------|---------------------------|
132: | `prevent-overengineering.md` | "build less" becoming licence to under-deliver frozen scope |
133: | `delegation-and-orchestration.md` | "orchestrate it" becoming licence to delegate everything |
134: | `communication.md` | "match length to the question" becoming licence to omit what the reader needs |
135: | `communication-decisions.md` | "verdict first" becoming licence to reason less before writing |
136: | `communication-handoff.md` | "name what is left" becoming licence to ask more, or to hand back your own unfinished work |

139: "fix the producer, not the symptom" as permission to do less.
140:

142: explicitly. If no, the section would be ceremony.
143: 
144: ---
145:

147:

149:

151:   everywhere else; a rule that does it is holding others to a bar it fails.
152: - **Don't restate another rule.** Link instead — and expect not to need to.

154:   A rule that fires on "thinking about testing" fires never.
155: - **Don't add a section because the rule looks short.** Length is not the target.
156: - **Don't write the self-check last and fastest.** It is the part a reader actually uses
157:   under time pressure, and it is where a rule most often stops being actionable.
158: 
159: ---
160: 
161: ## 8. WHAT THIS DOCUMENT IS NOT
162: 
163: - **Not a scoring rubric.** There is no number. Every test needs a reader, and a checkable
164:   proxy would measure the proxy.
165: - **Not licence to hold a draft to a bar the corpus does not meet.** Every test here passes
166:   on every shipped rule. A proposed sixth standard that they fail is a wrong standard.
167: 
168: ---
169: 
170: ## 9. SELF-CHECK
171: 
172: - [ ] For every section, I can say what breaks without it.
173: - [ ] No trigger phrase of mine appears in another rule.
174: - [ ] The binding sentence holds one obligation and stands alone.
175: - [ ] Every self-check item traces to a sentence in the body that created it.
176: - [ ] If the rule could be read as licence to do less, it says it is not.
177: - [ ] No best practice is cited without the failure it prevents.

57: runtime: it can be overridden by an explicit operator instruction, changed when it stops

67:   will delete after they stop being true.

69:   restraint ladder whose rung numbering contradicted the authoritative one. A review that
70:   only ever adds has not reviewed anything.

112: ---

38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal

58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```

71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
72: 
73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74:

76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```

202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
203: 
204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
205: 
206: **Core Purpose**:
207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
208: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
209: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216: 
217: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```
229: 
230: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.
231:

682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766:

769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible

885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```
995: 
996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:
997: ```python
998: def test_quick_mode():
999:     assert route_workflow("$quick fix").mode == "quick"
1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass
1006: 
1007: ---
1008: 
1009: ## 8. STANDARD STRUCTURE TEMPLATE
1010: 
1011: ### Complete Skill Directory Structure
1012: 
1013: **Path:** `.skilled/skills/` (singular, not `skills` or `openskills`)
1014: 
1015: ```
1016: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
1017: ├── SKILL.md                    # Main skill file (Level 2 in progressive disclosure)
1018: ├── references/                 # Deep-dive technical documentation (Level 3)
1019: │   ├── workflow-name.md        # Multi-phase workflows with checkpoints (kebab-case)
1020: │   ├── patterns-library.md     # Before/after code patterns (kebab-case)
1021: │   ├── debugging-guide.md      # Systematic troubleshooting (kebab-case)
1022: │   └── quick-reference.md      # Commands, shortcuts, checklists (kebab-case)
1023: ├── scripts/                    # Executable Python logic
1024: │   ├── mode_detection.py       # Procedural logic, algorithms
1025: │   ├── workflow_router.py      # Decision logic
1026: │   ├── config_validator.py     # Data transformation
1027: │   └── __init__.py             # Package initialization
1028: ├── assets/                     # Configuration and data files
1029: │   ├── workflow-configs/       # YAML workflow definitions
1030: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
1031: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
1032: │   ├── mappings/               # YAML mapping data
1033: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
1034: │   │   └── mode-recognition.yaml
1035: │   └── templates/              # Markdown/code templates
1036: │       ├── template-name.md
1037: │       └── component-template.tsx
1038: └── tests/                      # Unit and integration tests
1039:     ├── test_mode_detection.py
1040:     ├── test_workflow_router.py
1041:     ├── test_config_validator.py
1042:     └── __init__.py
1043: ```
1044: 
1045: ### Directory Purposes
1046: 
1047: **SKILL.md** (Required): Overview, workflow (3-5 steps), rules. Target: <200 lines
1048: 
1049: **references/** (Optional): Detailed workflows, patterns, debugging. Target: 500-3000 lines/file. **All authored filenames must use kebab-case.**
1050: 
1051: **scripts/** (Optional): Python logic - procedural, routing, validation. Requires type hints, tests
1052: 
1053: **assets/** (Optional): YAML configs, workflow definitions, templates, mappings
1054: 
1055: **tests/** (Required if scripts/ exists): Unit tests with ≥80% coverage, pytest, `test_[name].py`
1056: 
1057: ### When to Create Each Directory
1058: 
1059: | Directory     | Create When                                                     | Don't Create When                           |
1060: | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
1061: | `references/` | Content >200 lines, multi-phase workflows, systematic debugging | Simple skills <200 lines total              |
1062: | `scripts/`    | Python logic extracted from markdown, reusable functions        | Pure documentation, no executable logic     |
1063: | `assets/`     | YAML configs, templates, structured data                        | No configuration data, inline examples only |
1064: | `tests/`      | `scripts/` directory exists                                     | No Python scripts to test                   |
1065: 
1066: ### Integration Pattern
1067: 
1068: **How components work together:**
1069: - SKILL.md references scripts: `[workflow_router.py](./scripts/workflow_router.py)`
1070: - Scripts load configs: `yaml.safe_load(f"../assets/config.yaml")`
1071: - Tests verify scripts: `assert route_workflow("input").mode == "expected"`
1072: - Markdown links to all: "See [script.py](../scripts/), [config.yaml](../assets/)"
1073:

14: # Skill Reference File Templates - AI Agent Skills
15: 
16: Templates for creating reference files in AI agent skills with deep-dive technical guidance.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Location & Naming
23: 
24: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/references/`
25: 
26: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only
27: 
28: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
29: |---------------|-----------------|
30: | `implementation-workflows.md` | `ImplementationWorkflows.md` (PascalCase) |
31: | `tool-catalog.md` | `tool_catalog.md` (snake_case) |
32: | `debugging-guide.md` | `DebuggingGuide.MD` (wrong case) |
33: | `quick-reference.md` | `quickReference.md` (camelCase) |
34: | `code-quality-standards.md` | `code quality standards.md` (spaces) |
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
69: 
70: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
72: 
73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74: 
75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```
95: 
96: #### BAD Intro Structure (duplicates content)
97: 
98: ```markdown
99: # Git Commit Workflows
100: 
101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
102: 
103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
104: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
105: 
106: ### When to Use      ← WRONG: This belongs in Section 1!
107: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: \## 1. OVERVIEW
112: 
113: ### Purpose
114: Provides systematic workflows...  ← Now this duplicates the intro!
115: 
116: ### Core Principle
117: Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!
118: ```
119: 
120: #### Intro vs Section 1 Content Placement
121: 
122: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | Section 1 OVERVIEW |
123: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
124: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat) |
125: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
126: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
127: | Primary Sources       | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (as "Key Sources") |
128: | Purpose (detailed)    | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
129: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
130: | Any H3 subsections    | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES              |
131: 
132: ---
133: 
134: ### Reference Body Skeleton
135: 
136: **Every reference body follows this order.** The hook and the Purpose say different things: the hook names the job, and the Purpose names the outcome.
137: 
138: ```markdown
139: # [Title]
140: 
141: [1-2 sentence hook: what this reference covers and when to reach for it.]
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 1. OVERVIEW
146: 
147: ### Purpose
148: 
149: [The outcome this reference produces, in one or two sentences.]
150: 
151: ### When to Use
152: 
153: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
154: - [Second trigger]
155: 
156: ### Core Principle
157: 
158: [One-line statement that governs every rule below.]
159: 
160: ### Boundaries
161: 
162: - **In scope**: [What this reference owns]
163: - **Out of scope**: [What belongs in a sibling reference]
164: 
165: ### Key Sources
166: 
167: - [title](url) - [What the source establishes]
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 2. [CONTENT SECTION]
172: 
173: ### [Rule Group]
174: 
175: - **Rule:** [What to do]
176: - **Why:** [The failure it prevents]
177: - **Check:** [How to verify it]
178: 
179: ---
180: 
181: ## 3. [CONTENT SECTION]
182: 
183: [Body of the section]
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 4. RELATED RESOURCES
188: 
189: - [title](./sibling-reference.md) - [What the reader gets there]
190: ```
191: 
192: **Rules the skeleton encodes:**
193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.
194: - Content sections use integer numbers only: `## 2.`, `## 3.`, and so on.
195: - Rule fields are `- **Label:** text` bullets, never two bold labels on consecutive lines.
196: - Links are `[title](url)`, never a bare URL.
197: - Every `---` has a blank line above it, so a divider never turns the line above into a setext heading.
198: - A related section, when present, is the last H2.

202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
203: 
204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
205: 
206: **Core Purpose**:
207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
208: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
209: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216: 
217: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```
229: 
230: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.
231:

234: ## 3. WHEN TO CREATE REFERENCE FILES

238: **Workflow Complexity**:

244: **Technical Depth**:
245: - Root cause analysis required
246: - Tool integration details (MCP, scripts)
247: - Before/after code transformations
248: - Common error patterns and fixes

250: **Size Threshold**:

252: - Multiple related workflows
253: - Extensive troubleshooting needed

257: **Core Content**:
258: - Overview and "When to Use"
259: - High-level workflow (3-5 steps)
260: - Essential rules (ALWAYS/NEVER/ESCALATE IF)

262: - Quick reference

264: **Size**: Content under 200 lines

281: ## 4. AI AGENT SKILL REFERENCE CHARACTERISTICS
282: 
283: ### Core Principle Statements
284: 
285: **Purpose**: Distill philosophy into one-line wisdom

287: > **PLACEMENT**: Core Principle goes in **Section 1 OVERVIEW**, NOT in the intro paragraph after the H1 title.

290: ```markdown
291: \## 1. OVERVIEW
292: 
293: ### Purpose
294: 
295: [The outcome this reference produces]
296: 
297: ### When to Use
298: 
299: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]

301: ### Core Principle
302: 
303: [Single powerful statement that captures the workflow's essence]

306: **Examples from Real Skills**:
307: - "Wait for the actual condition you care about, not a guess about how long it takes"
308: - "ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure"

311: ### Phased Workflows with Validation
312:

682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766:

769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible

885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```
995: 
996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:
997: ```python
998: def test_quick_mode():
999:     assert route_workflow("$quick fix").mode == "quick"
1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass

14: # SKILL.md File Templates - Creation Guide
15: 
16: Templates for creating SKILL.md files with proper structure, frontmatter, and required sections.

18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose of SKILL.md Files
23: 
24: SKILL.md files define AI agent skills - reusable capabilities that extend an agent's functionality for specific domains or workflows. A well-crafted SKILL.md:
25: 
26: - **Triggers automatically** when relevant patterns are detected
27: - **Guides the agent** through specialized workflows
28: - **Maintains consistency** across conversations
29: - **Encodes expertise** in specific domains
30: 
31: ### Template Overview
32: 
33: This guide provides **one comprehensive SKILL template** (Section 3) that covers all skill types from simple single-purpose tools to complex multi-mode orchestrators.
34: 
35: **The template is flexible:**
36: - **Simple skills**: Use required core sections only (WHEN TO USE, SMART ROUTING, HOW IT WORKS, RULES, REFERENCES)
37: - **Skills with bundled resources**: Say in Section 2 what selects the skill and what it loads first, and put the router in the sibling `ROUTER.md`. Use `references/`, `assets/`, and `scripts/`
38: - **Multi-mode skills**: Expand WHEN TO USE and HOW IT WORKS sections by mode
39: - **All skills**: Section 2 (SMART ROUTING) is required: 8 to 12 non-blank lines of plain prose
40: 
41: **Target size**: 800-2000 lines for SKILL.md (<5k words total)
42: 
43: **Examples**:
44: - Simple: Unit test generator, documentation formatter (no bundled resources)
45: - Moderate: API client, specialized code reviewer (with references and assets)
46: - Complex: Workflow orchestrator, document quality pipeline (multi-mode with extensive resources)
47: 
48: ### Progressive Disclosure Principle
49: 
50: SKILL.md architecture follows progressive disclosure:
51: 
52: 1. **Metadata** (YAML frontmatter) - Always in context (~100 words)
53: 2. **SKILL.md body** - When skill activates (<5k words)
54: 3. **Bundled resources** - Loaded as needed (unlimited size)
55: 
56: **Critical**: Keep SKILL.md <5k words. Move detailed content to `references/`, `scripts/`, or `assets/`.
57: 
58: ### Document Type Requirements
59: 
60: **Enforcement Level**: STRICT (SKILL.md files require perfect structure)
61: 
62: **Required Elements**:
63: - ✅ YAML frontmatter with required fields
64: - ✅ H1 title with subtitle
65: - ✅ Numbered H2 sections (ALL CAPS, integers only, never a letter suffix such as `2b.`)
66: - ✅ Section separators (`---`)
67: - ✅ No table of contents (forbidden in SKILL.md)
68: 
69: **Quality Targets**:
70: - Structure: 100/100
71: - Content quality: High (AI-evaluated)
72: - Overall: High (human/AI judgment)

76: ## 2. FRONTMATTER REQUIREMENTS
77: 
78: ### Required Fields
79: 
80: | Field | Required | Format | Example |
81: |-------|----------|--------|---------|
82: | `name` | ✅ | hyphen-case | `my-skill-name` |
83: | `description` | ✅ | Single line, **≤ 130 chars** for skills (≤ 110 for commands), 1,536-char hard cap | `"Handles X when Y occurs"` |
84: | `allowed-tools` | ✅ | Array: `[Tool1, Tool2]` | `[Read, Write, Edit, Bash]` |
85: | `version` | ✅ | 4-part X.Y.Z.W | `1.0.0.0` |
86: 
87: > **Hard rules**: not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside the skill's `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects that the dispatch preflight reads.
88: 
89: > **Description budget & trim style**: see [`frontmatter-templates.md` § Description Budget & Trim Style](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md).
90: > Keep total project descriptions under the ~6,400-character ceiling. This leaves headroom below the 8,000-character auto-discovery limit.
91: > Drop product and stack lists. Drop marketing prose. Keep the skill name, primary verb, domain noun and mode suffixes (`:auto` or `:confirm`).
92: 
93: ### Template
94: 
95: ```yaml
96: ---
97: name: sk-example
98: description: Example workflow skill demonstrating proper frontmatter format with specific capabilities, use cases, and key differentiators for AI agent discovery.
99: allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep]
100: version: 1.0.0.0
101: ---
102: ```

104: ### Key Rules

423: ```

426: └── Bundled Resources

428:     ├── references/       - Detailed documentation (flat or domain subfolders)
429:     └── assets/           - Templates and examples (subfolders OK)

435: - **references/** = flat for small skills, domain subfolders for medium/complex skills
436:   - Flat example: `references/core-standards.md`, `references/validation.md`
437:   - Domain example: `references/backend/go/`, `references/frontend/react/`
438: - **assets/** = Subfolders ALLOWED when organizing many files by category
439:   - Group related templates together
440:   - Example: `assets/skill/`, `assets/readme/`, `assets/flowcharts/`
441: - **scripts/** = Typically flat, but subfolders OK for large script collections

444: - Skills auto-discovered from `.skilled/skills/*/SKILL.md` frontmatter
445: - Skill name in frontmatter MUST match folder name
